# Multidrug-resistant organism infections

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Multidrug-resistant organism infections*

[Original Article Link](/library/av0QA3)

---

## Summary

<u>Multidrug-resistant organisms</u> (<u>MDROs</u>) are pathogens, usually bacteria, that are resistant to one or more agent in three or more antimicrobial categories. <u>MDRO</u> infections result in increased hospital stay and mortality. The most common <u>MDROs</u> include <u>methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus</u>, <u>vancomycin-resistant enterococci</u>, and certain multidrug-resistant gram-negative microorganisms. The numerous <u>risk factors</u> for developing <u>MDRO</u> infections include health care exposure and prior use of antimicrobials. The treatment of <u>MDRO</u> infections is often complicated due to the limited antimicrobial options and is guided by <u>antibiotic</u> susceptibilities and the site and severity of infection. Measures for <u>infection prevention and control</u> are an essential part of <u>MDRO</u> management.

---

## Common gram-positive bacteria

### Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (<u>MRSA</u>) [[9]](/library/9udNt70)[[13]](/library/TJd6tI0)




<u>MRSA</u> infection can be <u>nosocomial</u> or community-acquired.




* Resistance

* All <u>β-lactam antibiotics</u> (i.e., <u>penicillins</u>, <u>cephalosporins</u>, <u>monobactams</u>, and <u>carbapenems</u>)

* <u>S. aureus</u> may also be resistant to the following (unrelated to <u>methicillin</u> resistance):

* <u>Aminoglycosides</u>

* <u>Macrolides</u>

* <u>Lincosamides</u>

* <u>Quinolones</u>

* <u>Glycopeptides</u> (e.g., <u>vancomycin-resistant S. aureus</u>)

* Mechanism of resistance: The staphylococcal mecA <u>gene</u> encodes a modified <u>penicillin-binding protein</u> (<u>PBP</u>) that inhibits the binding of <u>β-lactam antibiotics</u>. [[14]](/library/efbxOG)





> [!TIP]
> <u>MRSA</u> infections should always be treated; decolonization may be considered in certain individuals (e.g., those admitted to the <u>ICU</u> or with recurrent <u>MRSA</u> infections). [[15]](/library/8JdODI0)




> [!NOTE]
> The resistance mechanism of <u>MRSA</u> relies on modified <u>PBPs</u>, not on the production of <u>β-lactamase</u>.




### Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (<u>VRE</u>) [[9]](/library/9udNt70)[[16]](/library/gJdFtI0)[[17]](/library/SJdytI0)




* Pathogens: bacterial strains of the genus <u>Enterococcus</u> (e.g., <u>E. faecalis</u>, <u>E. faecium</u>)

* Resistance

* <u>Vancomycin</u> (possibly also <u>teicoplanin</u>)

* <u>Enterococci</u> may also be resistant to the following (unrelated to <u>vancomycin</u> resistance):

* <u>Macrolides</u>

* Most <u>penicillins</u> (<u>intrinsic resistance</u> to <u>penicillinase-resistant penicillins</u>, such as <u>oxacillin</u>, and <u>cephalosporins</u>)

* <u>Quinolones</u> (acquired or <u>intrinsic resistance</u>)

* <u>Aminoglycosides</u> (<u>intrinsic resistance</u>)

* <u>Tetracyclines</u>

* Mechanism of resistance

* Bacterial strains of the genus <u>Enterococcus</u> acquire <u>van genes</u> (e.g., through transposition of <u>plasmid</u>-encoded <u>genes</u> such as the vanA gene).

* <u>Van genes</u> (e.g., <u>vanA gene</u>) alter <u>peptidoglycan</u> synthesis (e.g., changing the D-<u>alanine</u>-D-<u>alanine</u> sequence to D-<u>alanine</u>-D-<u>lactate</u>), inhibiting <u>vancomycin</u> from binding to <u>peptidoglycans</u>.

---

## Common gram-negative bacteria

### Enterobacterales




#### ESBL-producing bacteria [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)




Bacteria that produce <u>extended-spectrum β-lactamase</u> (<u>ESBL</u>) cause multiple diseases, including <u>nosocomial UTIs</u> and <u>health care-associated pneumonia</u>.




* Pathogens: <u>gram-negative bacteria</u> that carry the <u>ESBL</u> <u>gene</u> (e.g., <u>Enterobacteriaceae</u> such as <u>Klebsiella</u> spp., <u>Escherichia coli</u>)

* Resistance

* <u>Penicillins</u>

* <u>Cephalosporins</u>

* <u>Aztreonam</u>

* Mechanism of resistance

* Production of <u>ESBL</u> that cleaves <u>penicillins</u>, <u>cephalosporins</u>, and <u>monobactam</u>

* Other mechanisms (e.g., changes in <u>outer membrane</u> <u>proteins</u>) can lead to <u>ertapenem</u> resistance. Resistance to <u>carbapenems</u> is rare. [[18]](/library/3JdSFI0)





#### <u>AmpC β-lactamase</u>-producing bacteria [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)[[19]](/library/OJdI8I0)




* Pathogens: most commonly <u>Enterobacter</u> cloacae complex, Citrobacter freundii, <u>Klebsiella aerogenes</u>

* Resistance

* <u>Penicillins</u> (e.g., <u>amoxicillin</u>)

* <u>Cephalosporins</u> (except for <u>cefepime</u>)

* <u>Monobactam</u> (e.g., <u>aztreonam</u>)

* Mechanism of resistance

* Production of AmpC that <u>hydrolyzes</u> <u>β-lactam antibiotics</u>

* AmpC β-lactamase production can be induced by exposure to certain <u>β-lactam antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>amoxicillin</u>, <u>ceftriaxone</u>).





#### <u>Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales</u> (<u>CRE</u>) [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)[[9]](/library/9udNt70)




* Pathogens: bacteria in the order Enterobacterales (e.g., <u>E. coli</u>, <u>K. pneumoniae</u>)

* Resistance

* ≥ 1 <u>carbapenem</u>

* <u>CRE</u> may additionally be resistant to <u>penicillins</u>, <u>cephalosporins</u>, and/or <u>aztreonam</u>.

* Mechanism of resistance, e.g.: [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)[[20]](/library/lJdv8I0)

* Noncarbapenemase <u>β-lactamase</u> (e.g., <u>ESBL</u>): causes <u>outer membrane</u> <u>porin</u> disruption

* Carbapenemases (e.g., <u>K. pneumoniae</u> carbapenemases, New Delhi metallo-<u>β-lactamase</u>): <u>hydrolyzes</u> almost all <u>β-lactam antibiotics</u>





### Multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)[[9]](/library/9udNt70)




<u>P. aeruginosa</u> causes multiple diseases, e.g., <u>pneumonia</u>, severe <u>soft tissue infections</u> (in infected wounds), <u>UTIs</u>, otitis external, and <u>keratitis</u>.




* Resistance

* <u>MDR P. aeruginosa</u>: resistance to ≥ 1 <u>antibiotic</u> in ≥ 3 generally susceptible <u>antibiotic</u> classes (i.e., <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, <u>penicillins</u>, <u>cephalosporins</u>, <u>aminoglycosides</u>, and <u>carbapenems</u>) [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)

* <u>P. aeruginosa</u>: <u>intrinsic resistance</u> to several <u>antibiotics</u> (e.g., most <u>penicillins</u>, most <u>cephalosporins</u>, and <u>macrolides</u>) [[21]](/library/kGdmzr0)[[22]](/library/4Gd3zr0)

* Mechanism of resistance: multiple mechanisms (e.g., decreased expression of <u>porins</u> in <u>outer membrane</u>, increased efflux pumps, <u>ESBL</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>P. aeruginosa</u> has a high level of <u>intrinsic resistance</u> to <u>antibiotics</u>.




### <u>Acinetobacter baumannii</u> [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)




* Resistance

* <u>MDR</u> <u>A. baumannii</u>: ≥ 1 agent in ≥ 3 <u>antibiotic</u> categories used to treat Acinetobacter infections (i.e., <u>cephalosporins</u>, <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, <u>aminoglycosides</u>, <u>carbapenems</u>, <u>piperacillin/tazobactam</u>, <u>ampicillin/sulbactam</u>) [[5]](/library/UFdbh70)

* <u>Carbapenem</u>-resistant <u>A. baumannii</u>: ≥ 1 <u>carbapenems</u> used to treat Acinetobacter infections (i.e., <u>imipenem</u>, <u>meropenem</u>, <u>doripenem</u>) [[5]](/library/UFdbh70)

* Mechanisms of resistance, e.g.: [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)[[9]](/library/9udNt70)[[23]](/library/2FdTh70)

* Enzymes (e.g., OXA carbapenemases, <u>serine</u> <u>β-lactamases</u>, <u>aminoglycoside</u>-modifying enzymes)

* Alterations in <u>outer membrane</u> <u>proteins</u> and <u>PBPs</u>, efflux pumps

* Genetic mutations

---

## Management

### General principles [[6]](/library/8pdOrI0)[[10]](/library/ZJdZsI0)




* Engage <u>antibiotic stewardship</u> programs during <u>antibiotic therapy</u> selection and initiation.

* Consider infectious diseases consult in infections due to <u>MDROs</u>, especially in cases of <u>carbapenem</u>-resistant organisms.

* Select <u>antibiotic therapy</u> based on the <u>pathogen</u>, <u>antibiotic</u> susceptibilities, and site and severity of the infection.

* <u>Antibiotics</u> to which the <u>MDRO</u> has resistance may still be effective at higher doses, increased frequency, and/or extended infusions.  [[25]](/library/bTcH6b0)

* A combination of multiple <u>antibiotics</u> may be needed.

* Implement measures for <u>infection prevention and control</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Antibiotic</u> regimens for the same <u>pathogen</u> may differ based on the infection site and severity.




### <u>Antimicrobial therapy</u>




Dosages depend on the specific disease and severity.

### Infection prevention [[10]](/library/ZJdZsI0)




* <u>Standard precautions</u>

* <u>Isolation precautions</u> (e.g., in acute care settings) [[31]](/library/CZ1qd20)

* Report <u>notifiable diseases</u> to the local health department.

* See also “<u>Prevention of common health care-associated infections</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Certain <u>MDROs</u> (e.g., <u>carbapenem</u>-resistant microorganisms, <u>vancomycin-resistant S. aureus</u>, <u>C. auris</u>) are reportable in the US. [[10]](/library/ZJdZsI0)




### Decolonization [[10]](/library/ZJdZsI0)[[15]](/library/8JdODI0)




* Not routinely recommended

* May be used in selected settings (e.g., patients in the <u>ICU</u>, preoperative) for <u>MRSA</u> eradication with either:

* <u>Mupirocin</u> nasal ointment

* <u>Chlorhexidine gluconate</u> baths  [[32]](/library/TFd6h70)
